## `inline_attribute_width`

Write an item and its attribute on the same line if their combined width is below a threshold

- **Default value**: 0
- **Possible values**: any nonnegative integer
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3343](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3343))
### Example

#### `0` (default):

```rust
#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
use core::slice;
```

#### `50`:

```rust
#[cfg(feature = "alloc")] use core::slice;
```

## `match_arm_blocks`

Controls whether arm bodies are wrapped in cases where the first line of the body cannot fit on the same line as the `=>` operator.

The Style Guide requires that bodies are block wrapped by default if a line break is required after the `=>`, but this option can be used to disable that behavior to prevent wrapping arm bodies in that event, so long as the body contains neither multiple statements nor line comments.

- **Default value**: `true`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3373](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3373))

#### `false`:

```rust
fn main() {
    match lorem {
        lorem =>
            foooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooo(x),
        ipsum => println!("{}", sit),
        sit => foo(
            "foooooooooooooooooooooooo",
            "baaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaarr",
            "baaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaazzzzzzzzzzzzz",
            "qqqqqqqqquuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuxxx",
        ),
    }
}
```

See also: [`match_block_trailing_comma`](#match_block_trailing_comma).

## `match_arm_leading_pipes`

Controls whether to include a leading pipe on match arms

- **Default value**: `"Never"`
- **Possible values**: `"Always"`, `"Never"`, `"Preserve"`
- **Stable**: Yes

## `match_arm_indent`

Controls whether match arms are indented.  If disabled, match arms will be formatted at the same indentation level as the outer `match` statement.  Meaning that match blocks will only be indented once, not twice.

- **Default value**: `true`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#6533](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/6533))

## `match_block_trailing_comma`

Put a trailing comma after a block based match arm (non-block arms are not affected)

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: Yes

## `max_width`

Maximum width of each line

- **Default value**: `100`
- **Possible values**: any nonnegative integer
- **Stable**: Yes

See also [`error_on_line_overflow`](#error_on_line_overflow).

## `merge_derives`

Merge multiple derives into a single one.

- **Default value**: `true`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: Yes

#### `true` (default):

```rust
#[derive(Eq, PartialEq, Debug, Copy, Clone)]
pub enum Foo {}
```

#### `false`:

```rust
#[derive(Eq, PartialEq, Debug, Copy, Clone)]
pub enum Bar {}

#[derive(Eq, PartialEq)]
#[derive(Debug)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone)]
pub enum Foo {}
```

## `imports_granularity`

Controls how imports are structured in `use` statements. Imports will be merged or split to the configured level of granularity.

Similar to other `import` related configuration options, this option operates within the bounds of user-defined groups of imports. See [`group_imports`](#group_imports) for more information on import groups.

Note that rustfmt will not modify the granularity of imports containing comments if doing so could potentially lose or misplace said comments.

- **Default value**: `Preserve`
- **Possible values**: `Preserve`, `Crate`, `Module`, `Item`, `One`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#4991](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/4991))

## `merge_imports`

This option is deprecated. Use `imports_granularity = "Crate"` instead.

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3362](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3362))

#### `true`:

```rust
use foo::{a, b, c, d, e, f, g};
```

## `newline_style`

Unix or Windows line endings

- **Default value**: `"Auto"`
- **Possible values**: `"Auto"`, `"Native"`, `"Unix"`, `"Windows"`
- **Stable**: Yes

#### `Auto` (default):

The newline style is detected automatically on a per-file basis. Files
with mixed line endings will be converted to the first detected line
ending style.

#### `Native`

Line endings will be converted to `\r\n` on Windows and `\n` on all
other platforms.

#### `Unix`

Line endings will be converted to `\n`.

#### `Windows`

Line endings will be converted to `\r\n`.

## `normalize_comments`

Convert /* */ comments to // comments where possible

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3350](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3350))

## `normalize_doc_attributes`

Convert `#![doc]` and `#[doc]` attributes to `//!` and `///` doc comments.

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3351](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3351))

## `overflow_delimited_expr`

When structs, slices, arrays, and block/array-like macros are used as the last
argument in an expression list, allow them to overflow (like blocks/closures)
instead of being indented on a new line.

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3370](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3370))

## `remove_nested_parens`

Remove nested parens.

- **Default value**: `true`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: Yes

## `reorder_impl_items`

Reorder impl items. `type` and `const` are put first, then macros and methods.

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3363](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3363))

## `reorder_imports`

Reorder import and extern crate statements alphabetically in groups (a group is
separated by a newline).

- **Default value**: `true`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: Yes

## `group_imports`

Controls the strategy for how consecutive imports are grouped together.

Controls the strategy for grouping sets of consecutive imports. Imports may contain newlines between imports and still be grouped together as a single set, but other statements between imports will result in different grouping sets.

- **Default value**: `Preserve`
- **Possible values**: `Preserve`, `StdExternalCrate`, `One`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#5083](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/5083))

Each set of imports (one or more `use` statements, optionally separated by newlines) will be formatted independently. Other statements such as `mod ...` or `extern crate ...` will cause imports to not be grouped together.

## `reorder_modules`

Reorder `mod` declarations alphabetically in group.

- **Default value**: `true`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: Yes

## `required_version`

Require a specific version of rustfmt. If you want to make sure that the
specific version of rustfmt is used in your CI, use this option.

- **Default value**: `CARGO_PKG_VERSION`
- **Possible values**: `semver` compliant values, such as defined on [semver.org](https://semver.org/).
  A value with no comparator, such as `"1.0.0"`, defaults to a caret (`^`)
  requirement, matching how Cargo treats dependency version requirements.
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3386](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3386))

heading_path: New minor or patch versions (default behavior):
sections.body:
#### New minor or patch versions (default behavior):

```toml
required_version="^1.0.0"
```

This is the default behavior, so that is equivalent to:

```toml
required_version="1.0.0"
```

#### Match on exact version:

```toml
required_version="=1.0.0"
```

#### Higher or equal to:

```toml
required_version=">=1.0.0"
```

#### Lower or equal to:

```toml
required_version="<=1.0.0"
```

#### New minor or patch versions:

```toml
required_version="^1.0.0"
```

#### New patch versions:

```toml
required_version="~1.0.0"
```

#### Wildcard:

```toml
required_version="*" # matches any version.
required_version="1.*" # matches any version with the same major version
required_version="1.0.*" # matches any version with the same major and minor version
```

#### Multiple versions to match:

A comma separated list of version requirements.
The match succeeds when the current rustfmt version matches all version requirements.

The one notable exception is that a wildcard matching any version cannot be used in the list.
For example, `*, <1.0.0` will always fail.

Additionally, the version match will always fail if any of the version requirements contradict themselves.
Some examples of contradictory requirements are `1.*, >2.0.0`, `1.0.*, >2.0.0` and `<1.5.0, >1.10.*`.

```toml
required_version=">=1.0.0, <2.0.0"
```

## `short_array_element_width_threshold`

The width threshold for an array element to be considered "short".

The layout of an array is dependent on the length of each of its elements. 
If the length of every element in an array is below this threshold (all elements are "short") then the array can be formatted in the mixed/compressed style, but if any one element has a length that exceeds this threshold then the array elements will have to be formatted vertically.

- **Default value**: `10`
- **Possible values**: any nonnegative integer that is less than or equal to the value specified for [`max_width`](#max_width)
- **Stable**: Yes

## `skip_children`

Don't reformat out of line modules

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3389](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3389))

## `single_line_if_else_max_width`

Maximum line length for single line if-else expressions. A value of `0` (zero) results in if-else expressions always being broken into multiple lines. Note this occurs when `use_small_heuristics` is set to `Off`.

- **Default value**: `50`
- **Possible values**: any nonnegative integer that is less than or equal to the value specified for [`max_width`](#max_width)
- **Stable**: Yes

By default this option is set as a percentage of [`max_width`](#max_width) provided by [`use_small_heuristics`](#use_small_heuristics), but a value set directly for `single_line_if_else_max_width` will take precedence.

See also [`max_width`](#max_width) and [`use_small_heuristics`](#use_small_heuristics)

## `single_line_let_else_max_width`

Maximum line length for single line let-else statements.
See the [let-else statement section of the Rust Style Guide](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/HEAD/src/doc/style-guide/src/statements.md#else-blocks-let-else-statements) for more details on when a let-else statement may be written on a single line.
A value of `0` (zero) means the divergent `else` block will always be formatted over multiple lines.
Note this occurs when `use_small_heuristics` is set to `Off`.

By default this option is set as a percentage of [`max_width`](#max_width) provided by [`use_small_heuristics`](#use_small_heuristics), but a value set directly for `single_line_let_else_max_width` will take precedence.

- **Default value**: `50`
- **Possible values**: any nonnegative integer that is less than or equal to the value specified for [`max_width`](#max_width)
- **Stable**: Yes

## `space_after_colon`

Leave a space after the colon.

- **Default value**: `true`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3366](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3366))

## `space_before_colon`

Leave a space before the colon.

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3365](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3365))

## `spaces_around_ranges`

Put spaces around the .., ..=, and ... range operators

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3367](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3367))

## `struct_field_align_threshold`

The maximum diff of width between struct fields to be aligned with each other.

- **Default value** : 0
- **Possible values**: any non-negative integer
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3371](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3371))

#### `0` (default):

```rust
struct Foo {
    x: u32,
    yy: u32,
    zzz: u32,
}
```

#### `20`:

```rust
struct Foo {
    x:   u32,
    yy:  u32,
    zzz: u32,
}
```

## `struct_lit_single_line`

Put small struct literals on a single line

- **Default value**: `true`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3357](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3357))

## `struct_lit_width`

Maximum width in the body of a struct literal before falling back to vertical formatting. A value of `0` (zero) results in struct literals always being broken into multiple lines. Note this occurs when `use_small_heuristics` is set to `Off`.

- **Default value**: `18`
- **Possible values**: any nonnegative integer that is less than or equal to the value specified for [`max_width`](#max_width)
- **Stable**: Yes

By default this option is set as a percentage of [`max_width`](#max_width) provided by [`use_small_heuristics`](#use_small_heuristics), but a value set directly for `struct_lit_width` will take precedence.

See also [`max_width`](#max_width), [`use_small_heuristics`](#use_small_heuristics), and [`struct_lit_single_line`](#struct_lit_single_line)

## `struct_variant_width`

Maximum width in the body of a struct variant before falling back to vertical formatting. A value of `0` (zero) results in struct literals always being broken into multiple lines. Note this occurs when `use_small_heuristics` is set to `Off`.

- **Default value**: `35`
- **Possible values**: any nonnegative integer that is less than or equal to the value specified for [`max_width`](#max_width)
- **Stable**: Yes

By default this option is set as a percentage of [`max_width`](#max_width) provided by [`use_small_heuristics`](#use_small_heuristics), but a value set directly for `struct_variant_width` will take precedence.

See also [`max_width`](#max_width) and [`use_small_heuristics`](#use_small_heuristics)

## `style_edition`

Controls the edition of the [Rust Style Guide] to use for formatting ([RFC 3338])

- **Default value**: `"2015"`
- **Possible values**:
  - Stable values: `"2015"`, `"2018"`, `"2021"`, `"2024"`
  - Unstable values: `"2027"`
- **Stable**: Yes

This option is inferred from the [`edition`](#edition) if not specified.

See [Rust Style Editions] for details on formatting differences between style editions.
rustfmt has a default style edition of `2015` while `cargo fmt` infers the style edition from the `edition` set in `Cargo.toml`. This can lead to inconsistencies between `rustfmt` and `cargo fmt` if the style edition is not explicitly configured.

To ensure consistent formatting, it is recommended to specify the `style_edition` in a `rustfmt.toml` configuration file. For example:

```toml
style_edition = "2024"
```

Alternatively, you can use the `--style-edition` flag when running `rustfmt` directly.

[Rust Style Editions]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/style-guide/editions.html?highlight=editions#rust-style-editions
[Rust Style Guide]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/style-guide/
[RFC 3338]: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3338-style-evolution.html

## `tab_spaces`

Number of spaces per tab

- **Default value**: `4`
- **Possible values**: any nonnegative integer
- **Stable**: Yes

## `trailing_comma`

How to handle trailing commas for lists

- **Default value**: `"Vertical"`
- **Possible values**: `"Always"`, `"Never"`, `"Vertical"`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3379](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3379))

## `trailing_semicolon`

Add trailing semicolon after break, continue and return

- **Default value**: `true`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3378](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3378))

## `type_punctuation_density`

Determines if `+` or `=` are wrapped in spaces in the punctuation of types

- **Default value**: `"Wide"`
- **Possible values**: `"Compressed"`, `"Wide"`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3364](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3364))

## `unstable_features`

Enable unstable features on the unstable channel.

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3387](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3387))

## `use_field_init_shorthand`

Use field initialize shorthand if possible.

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: Yes

## `use_small_heuristics`

This option can be used to simplify the management and bulk updates of the granular width configuration settings ([`fn_call_width`](#fn_call_width), [`attr_fn_like_width`](#attr_fn_like_width), [`struct_lit_width`](#struct_lit_width), [`struct_variant_width`](#struct_variant_width), [`array_width`](#array_width), [`chain_width`](#chain_width), [`single_line_if_else_max_width`](#single_line_if_else_max_width)), that respectively control when formatted constructs are multi-lined/vertical based on width.

Note that explicitly provided values for the width configuration settings take precedence and override the calculated values determined by `use_small_heuristics`.

- **Default value**: `"Default"`
- **Possible values**: `"Default"`, `"Off"`, `"Max"`
- **Stable**: Yes

#### `Default` (default):

When `use_small_heuristics` is set to `Default`, the values for the granular width settings are calculated as a ratio of the value for `max_width`.

The ratios are:
* [`fn_call_width`](#fn_call_width) - `60%`
* [`attr_fn_like_width`](#attr_fn_like_width) - `70%`
* [`struct_lit_width`](#struct_lit_width) - `18%`
* [`struct_variant_width`](#struct_variant_width) - `35%`
* [`array_width`](#array_width) - `60%`
* [`chain_width`](#chain_width) - `60%`
* [`single_line_if_else_max_width`](#single_line_if_else_max_width) - `50%`
* [`single_line_let_else_max_width`](#single_line_let_else_max_width) - `50%`

For example when `max_width` is set to `100`, the width settings are:
* `fn_call_width=60`
* `attr_fn_like_width=70`
* `struct_lit_width=18`
* `struct_variant_width=35`
* `array_width=60`
* `chain_width=60`
* `single_line_if_else_max_width=50`
* `single_line_let_else_max_width=50`

and when `max_width` is set to `200`:
* `fn_call_width=120`
* `attr_fn_like_width=140`
* `struct_lit_width=36`
* `struct_variant_width=70`
* `array_width=120`
* `chain_width=120`
* `single_line_if_else_max_width=100`
* `single_line_let_else_max_width=100`

```rust
enum Lorem {
    Ipsum,
    Dolor(bool),
    Sit { amet: Consectetur, adipiscing: Elit },
}

fn main() {
    lorem(
        "lorem",
        "ipsum",
        "dolor",
        "sit",
        "amet",
        "consectetur",
        "adipiscing",
    );

    let lorem = Lorem {
        ipsum: dolor,
        sit: amet,
    };
    let lorem = Lorem { ipsum: dolor };

    let lorem = if ipsum { dolor } else { sit };
}
```

#### `Max`:

When `use_small_heuristics` is set to `Max`, then each granular width setting is set to the same value as `max_width`.

So if `max_width` is set to `200`, then all the width settings are also set to `200`.
* `fn_call_width=200`
* `attr_fn_like_width=200`
* `struct_lit_width=200`
* `struct_variant_width=200`
* `array_width=200`
* `chain_width=200`
* `single_line_if_else_max_width=200`
* `single_line_let_else_max_width=200`

```rust
enum Lorem {
    Ipsum,
    Dolor(bool),
    Sit { amet: Consectetur, adipiscing: Elit },
}

fn main() {
    lorem("lorem", "ipsum", "dolor", "sit", "amet", "consectetur", "adipiscing");

    let lorem = Lorem { ipsum: dolor, sit: amet };

    let lorem = if ipsum { dolor } else { sit };
}
```

See also:
* [`max_width`](#max_width)
* [`fn_call_width`](#fn_call_width)
* [`attr_fn_like_width`](#attr_fn_like_width)
* [`struct_lit_width`](#struct_lit_width)
* [`struct_variant_width`](#struct_variant_width)
* [`array_width`](#array_width)
* [`chain_width`](#chain_width)
* [`single_line_if_else_max_width`](#single_line_if_else_max_width)
* [`single_line_let_else_max_width`](#single_line_let_else_max_width)

## `use_try_shorthand`

Replace uses of the try! macro by the ? shorthand

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: Yes

## `version`

This option is deprecated and has been replaced by [`style_edition`](#style_edition).
`version = "One"` is equivalent to `style_edition = "(2015|2018|2021)"` and
`version = "Two"` is equivalent to `style_edition = "2024"`

- **Default value**: `One`
- **Possible values**: `One`, `Two`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3383](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3383))

### Example

```toml
version = "Two"
```

## `where_single_line`

Forces the `where` clause to be laid out on a single line.

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3359](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3359))

## `wrap_comments`

Break comments to fit on the line

Note that no wrapping will happen if:
1. The comment is the start of a markdown header doc comment
2. A URL was found in the comment
3. An inline link like fragment was found in the comment

- **Default value**: `false`
- **Possible values**: `true`, `false`
- **Stable**: No (tracking issue: [#3347](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/3347))
# Internal Options

## `emit_mode`

Internal option

## `make_backup`

Internal option, use `--backup`

## `print_misformatted_file_names`

Internal option, use `-l` or `--files-with-diff`

### What it does

Checks for .unwrap() or .unwrap_err() calls on Result s and .unwrap() call on Option s.

### Why restrict this?

It is better to handle the None or Err case, or at least call .expect(_) with a more helpful message. Still, for a lot of quick-and-dirty code, unwrap is a good choice, which is why this lint is Allow by default.

result.unwrap() will let the thread panic on Err values. Normally, you want to implement more sophisticated error handling, and propagate errors upwards with ? operator.

Even if you want to panic on errors, not all Error s implement good messages on display. Therefore, it may be beneficial to look at the places where they may get displayed. Activate this lint to do just that.

### Examples

```rust
option.unwrap();
result.unwrap();
```

Use instead:

```rust
option.expect("more helpful message");
result.expect("more helpful message");
```

If [expect_used](https://clippy.rust-lang.org/stable/index.html#expect_used) is enabled, instead:

```rust
option?;

// or

result?;
```

### Past names

- option_unwrap_used

- result_unwrap_used

### Configuration

- allow-unwrap-in-consts : Whether unwrap should be allowed in code always evaluated at compile time (default: true )

- allow-unwrap-in-tests : Whether unwrap should be allowed in test functions or #[cfg(test)] (default: false )

- allow-unwrap-types : List of types to allow unwrap() and expect() on.

#### Example

```
allow-unwrap-types = [ "std::sync::LockResult" ]
```

(default: [] )

### What it does

Checks for usage of .clone() on a Copy type.

### Why is this bad?

The only reason Copy types implement Clone is for generics, not for using the clone method on a concrete type.

### Example

```rust
42u64.clone();
```

### What it does

Checks for .expect() or .expect_err() calls on Result s and .expect() call on Option s.

### Why restrict this?

Usually it is better to handle the None or Err case. Still, for a lot of quick-and-dirty code, expect is a good choice, which is why this lint is Allow by default.

result.expect() will let the thread panic on Err values. Normally, you want to implement more sophisticated error handling, and propagate errors upwards with ? operator.

### Examples

```rust
option.expect("one");
result.expect("one");
```

Use instead:

```rust
option?;

// or

result?;
```

### Past names

- option_expect_used

- result_expect_used

### Configuration

- allow-expect-in-consts : Whether expect should be allowed in code always evaluated at compile time (default: true )

- allow-expect-in-tests : Whether expect should be allowed in test functions or #[cfg(test)] (default: false )

- allow-unwrap-types : List of types to allow unwrap() and expect() on.

#### Example

```
allow-unwrap-types = [ "std::sync::LockResult" ]
```

(default: [] )

### What it does

Checks for usage of panic! .

### Why restrict this?

This macro, or panics in general, may be unwanted in production code.

### Example

```rust
panic!("even with a good reason");
```

### Configuration

- allow-panic-in-tests : Whether panic should be allowed in test functions or #[cfg(test)] (default: false )

### What it does

Checks for while let expressions on iterators.

### Why is this bad?

Readability. A simple for loop is shorter and conveys the intent better.

### Example

```rust
while let Some(val) = iter.next() {
    ..
}
```

Use instead:

```rust
for val in &mut iter {
    ..
}
```

### What it does

Warn of cases where let...else could be used

### Why is this bad?

let...else provides a standard construct for this pattern that people can easily recognize. It’s also more compact.

### Example

```rust
let v = if let Some(v) = w { v } else { return };
```

Could be written:

```rust
let Some(v) = w else { return };
```

### Configuration

- matches-for-let-else : Whether the matches should be considered by the lint, and whether there should be filtering for common types. (default: "WellKnownTypes" )

- msrv : The minimum rust version that the project supports. Defaults to the rust-version field in Cargo.toml (default: current version )

### What it does

Checks for address of operations ( & ) that are going to be dereferenced immediately by the compiler.

### Why is this bad?

Suggests that the receiver of the expression borrows the expression.

### Known problems

The lint cannot tell when the implementation of a trait for &T and T do different things. Removing a borrow in such a case can change the semantics of the code.

### Example

```rust
fn fun(_a: &i32) {}

let x: &i32 = &&&&&&5;
fun(&x);
```

Use instead:

```rust
let x: &i32 = &5;
fun(x);
```

### Past names

- ref_in_deref

### Configuration

- msrv : The minimum rust version that the project supports. Defaults to the rust-version field in Cargo.toml (default: current version )

checklist.title: Casing conforms to RFC 430
Ad-hoc conversions follow as_, to_, into_ conventions
Getter names follow Rust convention
Methods on collections that produce iterators follow iter, iter_mut, into_iter
Iterator type names match the methods that produce them
Feature names are free of placeholder words
Names use a consistent word order
Types eagerly implement common traits
Conversions use the standard traits From, AsRef, AsMut
Collections implement FromIterator and Extend
Data structures implement Serde's Serialize, Deserialize
Types are Send and Sync where possible
Error types are meaningful and well-behaved
Binary number types provide Hex, Octal, Binary formatting
Generic reader/writer functions take R: Read and W: Write by value
Input syntax is evocative of the output
Macros compose well with attributes
Item macros work anywhere that items are allowed
Item macros support visibility specifiers
Type fragments are flexible
Crate level docs are thorough and include examples
All items have a rustdoc example
Examples use ?, not try!, not unwrap
Function docs include error, panic, and safety considerations
Prose contains hyperlinks to relevant things
Cargo.toml includes all common metadata
Release notes document all significant changes
Rustdoc does not show unhelpful implementation details
Smart pointers do not add inherent methods
Conversions live on the most specific type involved
Functions with a clear receiver are methods
Functions do not take out-parameters
Operator overloads are unsurprising
Only smart pointers implement Deref and DerefMut
Constructors are static, inherent methods
Functions expose intermediate results to avoid duplicate work
Caller decides where to copy and place data
Functions minimize assumptions about parameters by using generics
Traits are object-safe if they may be useful as a trait object
Newtypes provide static distinctions
Arguments convey meaning through types, not bool or Option
Types for a set of flags are bitflags, not enums
Builders enable construction of complex values
Functions validate their arguments
Destructors never fail
Destructors that may block have alternatives
All public types implement Debug
Debug representation is never empty
Sealed traits protect against downstream implementations
Structs have private fields
Newtypes encapsulate implementation details
Data structures do not duplicate derived trait bounds
Public dependencies of a stable crate are stable
Crate and its dependencies have a permissive license

commands.purpose: Create a new Cargo package in a new directory.
examples: `cargo new my-project` creates a `my-project/` directory containing a `Cargo.toml` and a `src/main.rs` (or `src/lib.rs` with `--lib`).
prerequisites: A Rust toolchain that includes `cargo` is installed (for example via `rustup`).
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo new --help` for the version-specific option list.

effect_notes.detail: creates a new project directory (a `Cargo.toml` and a `src/` file); it does not modify an existing project.

commands.purpose: Initialize a Cargo package in an existing directory.
examples: Running `cargo init` inside an existing directory writes a `Cargo.toml` (and a `src/` file) without overwriting existing files.
prerequisites: A Rust toolchain that includes `cargo` is installed (for example via `rustup`).
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo init --help` for the version-specific option list.

effect_notes.detail: writes a `Cargo.toml` (and a `src/` file) into the target directory; existing files are not overwritten.

commands.purpose: Emit metadata about the current package, workspace, or dependency graph as a machine-readable structure.
examples: `cargo metadata --format-version 1 --manifest-path Cargo.toml` prints the workspace metadata as JSON on stdout.
prerequisites: A Cargo project or workspace: a manifest (`Cargo.toml`) is present in the working directory or an ancestor of it.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; the `--format-version` must be supported by the installed `cargo` (run `cargo metadata --help` to list it).

commands.purpose: Print the path to the Cargo manifest that `cargo` resolves for the given (or current) location.
examples: Running `cargo locate-project` prints the path to the `Cargo.toml` that `cargo` would use from the current directory.
prerequisites: A Cargo project or workspace: `cargo` is run within (or below) a directory tree that contains a manifest.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo locate-project --help` for the version-specific option list.

commands.purpose: Display a tree of the dependencies of the current package or workspace.
examples: Running `cargo tree` prints the dependency tree; `cargo tree -p my-crate` restricts it to a single package.
prerequisites: A Cargo project with a manifest and a resolved dependency graph; run `cargo update` or `cargo generate-lockfile` to refresh `Cargo.lock` before inspecting it.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo tree --help` for the version-specific option list.

commands.purpose: Add a dependency to one of this package's manifest groups.
examples: `cargo add serde` adds `serde` to the `[dependencies]` group of the current package's `Cargo.toml`, resolving it against the configured sources and recording the chosen version in `Cargo.lock`.
`cargo add serde --features derive` records the `derive` feature in the manifest's feature selection for the dependency.
prerequisites: A Cargo package or workspace: a manifest (`Cargo.toml`) is present in the working directory or an ancestor of it.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo add --help` for the version-specific option list. The flags `--offline` and `--locked` are documented for this command: `--offline` resolves from the local cache only, and `--locked` asserts the lockfile will not be changed.

effect_notes.detail: writes the new dependency into `Cargo.toml` (a source change); it does not touch a package's own source files.
updates `Cargo.lock` with the resolved version; `--locked` asserts the lockfile will not be changed and errors otherwise, and `--offline` resolves from the local cache only.
may download the new dependency from a configured source; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) prevents any download.

commands.purpose: Remove dependencies from the manifest.
examples: `cargo remove serde` removes `serde` from the `[dependencies]` group of the current package's `Cargo.toml`.
prerequisites: A Cargo package or workspace: a manifest (`Cargo.toml`) is present in the working directory or an ancestor of it.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo remove --help` for the version-specific option list. The flags `--offline` and `--locked` are documented for this command: `--offline` resolves from the local cache only, and `--locked` asserts the lockfile will not be changed.

effect_notes.detail: removes the dependency entry from `Cargo.toml` (a source change); it does not touch a package's own source files.
may rewrite `Cargo.lock` to drop the removed package; `--locked` asserts the lockfile will not be changed and errors otherwise, and `--offline` resolves from the local cache only.
may download the remaining or replacement dependencies while re-resolving; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) prevents any download.

commands.purpose: Update dependencies as specified by the `Cargo.lock` file.
examples: `cargo update` refreshes `Cargo.lock` to the newest versions the manifest's requirements allow; `cargo update --precise 1.0.0` pins a specific dependency to `1.0.0` in the lockfile.
prerequisites: A Cargo package or workspace with a manifest; a `Cargo.lock` is read or created when re-resolving.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo update --help` for the version-specific option list. The flags `--offline` and `--locked` are documented for this command: `--offline` resolves from the local cache only, and `--locked` asserts the lockfile will not be changed.

effect_notes.detail: rewrites `Cargo.lock` with the newly resolved versions (a lockfile change; it does not edit `Cargo.toml`); `--locked` asserts the lockfile will not be changed and errors otherwise, and `--offline` resolves from the local cache only.
may download the newly resolved sources; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) prevents any download.

commands.purpose: Generate a `Cargo.lock` lockfile without building.
examples: `cargo generate-lockfile` resolves the package's dependencies against the configured sources and writes `Cargo.lock` without building or running any code.
prerequisites: A Cargo package or workspace: a manifest (`Cargo.toml`) is present in the working directory or an ancestor of it.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo generate-lockfile --help` for the version-specific option list. The flags `--offline` and `--locked` are documented for this command: `--offline` resolves from the local cache only, and `--locked` asserts the lockfile will not be changed.

effect_notes.detail: creates or refreshes `Cargo.lock` by resolving the manifest against the sources (a lockfile change; it does not edit `Cargo.toml`); `--locked` asserts the lockfile will not be changed and errors otherwise, and `--offline` resolves from the local cache only.
may download sources during resolution; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) prevents any download.

commands.purpose: Fetch all dependencies into the local cache.
examples: `cargo fetch` downloads every dependency the manifest resolves into the local cache, so later `cargo build` / `cargo check` / `cargo test` can run offline.
prerequisites: A Cargo package or workspace: a manifest (`Cargo.toml`) is present in the working directory or an ancestor of it.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo fetch --help` for the version-specific option list. The flag `--offline` is documented for this command: it makes the fetch use the local cache only.

effect_notes.detail: downloads the package's dependencies into the local cache; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) makes the fetch use the cache only (no network).
may update `Cargo.lock` to match the manifest when the lockfile is missing or out of date (a lockfile change; it does not edit `Cargo.toml`).

commands.purpose: Compile the current package to check for errors, without generating a final artifact.
examples: `cargo check` compiles the package to the point of type-checking and borrow-checking and reports errors, producing no final binary or library artifact; it is the fast path for iterative development.
prerequisites: A Cargo package or workspace: a manifest (`Cargo.toml`) is present in the working directory or an ancestor of it.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo check --help` for the version-specific option list. The selection flags `-p`/`--package`, `-w`/`--workspace`, `--target`, and `--features`/`--all-features` choose the package(s), target, and feature set to check; `--offline` resolves from the local cache only and `--locked` asserts the lockfile will not be changed.

`cargo check` does not execute a program, so it has no program-argument forwarding after `--`; compiler flags are supplied through `RUSTFLAGS` or the documented build options rather than a program-argument separator.

effect_notes.detail: writes intermediate build metadata to the `target/` directory; per its documented behavior it produces no final binary or library artifact and runs no code — the check side of the check-vs-apply distinction.
may download dependencies that are not yet cached; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) prevents any download.

commands.purpose: Compile the current package, producing its binary or library artifacts.
examples: `cargo build` compiles the current package and writes its artifacts (a binary for a `bin` target, a library for a `lib` target) under `target/`; `cargo build --release` builds an optimized release profile.
prerequisites: A Cargo package or workspace: a manifest (`Cargo.toml`) is present in the working directory or an ancestor of it.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo build --help` for the version-specific option list. The selection flags `-p`/`--package`, `-w`/`--workspace`, `--target`, and `--features`/`--all-features` choose the package(s), target, and feature set to build; `--offline` resolves from the local cache only and `--locked` asserts the lockfile will not be changed.

`cargo build` does not execute a program, so it has no program-argument forwarding after `--`; compiler flags are supplied through `RUSTFLAGS` or the documented build options rather than a program-argument separator.

effect_notes.detail: produces the final build artifacts (a binary and/or library) under `target/` — the build-output side effect that distinguishes `cargo build` from the check commands.
may download dependencies that are not yet cached; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) prevents any download.

commands.purpose: Compile and then execute the current package's binary.
examples: `cargo run` compiles the package and runs its binary; `cargo run -- --help` compiles the binary and forwards `--help` to the program — everything after `--` is the program's argument list.
prerequisites: A Cargo package with an executable target (`bin` or `example`): a manifest (`Cargo.toml`) is present in the working directory or an ancestor of it.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo run --help` for the version-specific option list. The selection flags `-p`/`--package`, `-w`/`--workspace`, `--target`, and `--features`/`--all-features` choose the package(s), target, and feature set to run; `--offline` resolves from the local cache only and `--locked` asserts the lockfile will not be changed.

Argument forwarding: everything after `--` is forwarded to the program being run, and nothing before `--` is (those are cargo options). This is the one of the compile commands that executes a program, so it is the one that forwards program arguments.

effect_notes.detail: compiles the package and then runs its own binary (its code executes) — the execute side of the family.
produces build artifacts under `target/` before running.
may download dependencies that are not yet cached; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) prevents any download.

commands.purpose: Compile and run the current package's tests, including the documentation tests (doctests).
examples: `cargo test` compiles and runs the package's unit, integration, and doctests; `cargo test --lib` runs only the library's unit tests and `cargo test --bins` only the binaries' tests.

`cargo test --doc` runs the documentation tests (doctests) only — the doctest-vs-other-tests distinction; a doctest is the fenced code in a `///` or `//!` doc comment that `cargo test --doc` compiles and runs.
prerequisites: A Cargo package or workspace with tests or doctests: a manifest (`Cargo.toml`) is present in the working directory or an ancestor of it.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo test --help` for the version-specific option list. The selection flags `-p`/`--package`, `-w`/`--workspace`, `--target`, and `--features`/`--all-features` choose the package(s), target, and feature set to test; `--offline` resolves from the local cache only and `--locked` asserts the lockfile will not be changed.

Doctests are the fenced code in doc comments: `cargo test` runs them together with the unit and integration tests, while `cargo test --doc` runs the doctests only. Arguments after `--` are forwarded to the test binary; `--lib`/`--bins`/`--tests`/`--doc` select which target types run.

effect_notes.detail: compiles and runs the package's tests — unit, integration, and doctests execute — the execute side of the family.
produces the test-binary artifacts under `target/`.
may download dependencies that are not yet cached; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) prevents any download.

commands.purpose: Compile and run the current package's benchmarks.
examples: `cargo bench` compiles and runs the package's `[[bench]]` targets; `cargo bench -- --exact` forwards `--exact` to the benchmark harness.
prerequisites: A Cargo package with a `[[bench]]` target (commonly the `criterion` crate): a manifest (`Cargo.toml`) is present in the working directory or an ancestor of it.
compatibility: `cargo bench` is a stable command. The built-in `#[bench]` test-harness macros were nightly-only and have since been removed; stable benchmarking today uses the `criterion` crate with a `[[bench]]` target — no nightly toolchain is required for `cargo bench` itself, and no nightly requirement is claimed that the documentation does not state.

Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo bench --help` for the version-specific option list. The selection flags `-p`/`--package`, `-w`/`--workspace`, `--target`, and `--features`/`--all-features` choose the package(s), target, and feature set to benchmark; `--offline` resolves from the local cache only. Arguments after `--` are forwarded to the benchmark binary.

effect_notes.detail: compiles and runs the package's benchmarks — their code executes.
produces the benchmark-binary artifacts under `target/`.
may download dependencies that are not yet cached; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) prevents any download.

commands.purpose: Run rustfmt on the current package to format its source code.
examples: `cargo fmt` runs rustfmt and rewrites the package's source files to the canonical formatting; `cargo fmt --check` (equivalently `-n`) reports what would change without writing — the check-vs-apply distinction for formatting.
`cargo fmt -- --config tab_spaces=4` forwards the rustfmt option after `--`; rustfmt's own options follow the separator, distinct from cargo's options before it.
prerequisites: A Rust toolchain that includes `rustfmt` (for example via the `rustup` default components).
compatibility: `cargo fmt` is a stable command that invokes `rustfmt`; only rustfmt's *unstable* options require a nightly rustfmt, not the command or its stable options. Cargo options (`--manifest-path`, `--all` / `--all-packages`, and `-p`/`--package`) select the package(s) to format and are distinct from rustfmt options, which follow `--`; `--target` and `--features` are not rustfmt options and are not forwarded to it.

effect_notes.detail: rustfmt rewrites the package's source files to apply canonical formatting (a source change); it does not change the program's behavior. `cargo fmt --check` (a.k.a. `-n`) performs the same analysis without writing.

commands.purpose: Run Clippy's lints on the current package to find things that can be simplified or done better.
examples: `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` compiles the package under Clippy's lints and treats warnings as errors; `cargo clippy --fix` instead applies the lints' machine-applicable suggestions.
prerequisites: A Rust toolchain that includes the `clippy` component (for example via `rustup`).
compatibility: `cargo clippy` is a stable command; Clippy runs on a stable toolchain, although a small number of lints are nightly-only. Lint levels are set with `-A`/`--allow`, `-W`/`--warn`, `-D`/`--deny`, and `-F`/`--forbid` (or by lint group, e.g. `clippy::pedantic`); `-D warnings` makes warnings fatal. The full, version-specific option list is in `cargo clippy --help`.

Clippy/compiler options are distinct from cargo options: clippy lint levels and rustc flags are forwarded after `--`, while the selection flags `-p`/`--package`, `-w`/`--workspace`, `--target`, and `--features`/`--all-features` and `--offline`/`--locked` are cargo options before it.

effect_notes.detail: compiles the package under Clippy's lints, writing build artifacts to `target/`; by default it *reports* lints and does not modify source — a check. `cargo clippy --fix` instead applies the machine-applicable suggestions.
may download dependencies that are not yet cached; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) prevents any download.

commands.purpose: Generate the current package's documentation by running rustdoc.
examples: `cargo doc` runs rustdoc and writes HTML documentation for the package's library and binaries to `target/doc`; `cargo doc --open` opens the result in a browser and `cargo doc -- --help` forwards `--help` to rustdoc.
prerequisites: A Rust toolchain that includes `rustdoc` (for example via `rustup`): a manifest (`Cargo.toml`) is present in the working directory or an ancestor of it.
compatibility: `cargo doc` is a stable command that invokes `rustdoc`; rustdoc options follow `--` and are distinct from cargo options. The selection flags `-p`/`--package`, `-w`/`--workspace`, `--target`, and `--features`/`--all-features` and `--offline`/`--locked` are cargo options. Doctests are *executed* by `cargo test`, not by `cargo doc`.

effect_notes.detail: runs rustdoc and writes generated HTML documentation under `target/doc` (an artifact); it does not modify the source tree and does not run the doctests.
may download dependencies that are not yet cached; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) prevents any download.

commands.purpose: Apply the fixes the compiler suggests for the current package's warnings.
examples: `cargo fix` runs the compiler with its suggestions and applies the machine-applicable fixes to the source; review the diff afterward. `cargo fix --broken-code` allows applying fixes that may leave the code non-compiling.
prerequisites: Run `cargo check` or `cargo build` first so the compiler has suggestions to apply; a manifest (`Cargo.toml`) is present in the working directory or an ancestor of it.
compatibility: `cargo fix` is a stable command that applies the compiler's own suggestions and requires no nightly toolchain. By default it refuses to leave the code in a non-compiling state; `--broken-code` relaxes that. The selection flags `-p`/`--package`, `-w`/`--workspace`, `--target`, and `--features`/`--all-features` are cargo options, and arguments after `--` are forwarded to the compiler.

effect_notes.detail: applies the compiler's suggested fixes to the package's source files (a source change — the apply counterpart to the check commands); review the diff after running, and use `--broken-code` only where a non-compiling intermediate is acceptable.
compiles the package to gather suggestions and may download dependencies that are not yet cached; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) prevents any download.

commands.purpose: Package the current package into a distributable `.crate` archive.
examples: `cargo package` verifies the current package and writes a distributable `.crate` tarball to `target/`; `cargo package --list` lists the files that would be included without creating the archive; `--no-verify` skips the verification build and `--allow-dirty` packs a working tree that has local changes.
prerequisites: A Cargo package with a complete manifest (`Cargo.toml`) whose `name`, `version`, and license are set: packaging verifies these before producing the archive.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo package --help` for the version-specific option list. `--list` lists the files that would be packaged without creating the archive, `--no-verify` skips the verification build, and `--allow-dirty` packs a working tree with local or uncommitted changes.

`cargo package` produces the distributable `.crate` archive but does not publish or upload it — uploading is `cargo publish`. Retrieving this entry is documentation lookup: it surfaces packaging guidance and does not authorize, request, or perform a publication; the calling agent decides whether to run `cargo package` (and, later, `cargo publish`) through its own terminal tools.

effect_notes.detail: produces a distributable `.crate` tarball under `target/` (the packaging artifact); it packages but does not publish or upload — uploading is `cargo publish`.
the default verification build may download dependencies that are not yet cached; `--offline` (or `--frozen`) prevents any download. `--no-verify` skips the verification build.

commands.purpose: Package and upload the current package to the configured registry.
examples: `cargo publish` packages the current package (as `cargo package` does) and uploads the resulting `.crate` to the configured registry; `cargo publish --dry-run` performs the same packaging and verification but does NOT upload — it reports what would be published.
prerequisites: A publishable package — a complete manifest, a valid version, and a registry name not already taken — plus registry authentication: a configured registry token or credential. The default registry is crates.io.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `cargo`; run `cargo publish --help` for the version-specific option list. The registry is selected with `--registry` and authenticated with `--token` (or a configured credential); `--no-verify` skips the verification build. `--dry-run` performs the packaging and verification but does NOT upload — it reports what would be published. Publishing is the *default* behavior: omitting `--dry-run` is what uploads, so `--dry-run` is the prepare-only form (there is no `--no-dry-run` flag — the default already publishes).

Release-preparation guidance is documentation lookup: retrieving this entry surfaces documentation and does not authorize, request, or perform a publication. No registry upload happens as a result of this lookup; the calling agent decides whether to run `cargo publish` through its own terminal tools. The effect note below names the possible publication effect; it is not an authorization.

effect_notes.detail: uploads the packaged `.crate` to the configured registry (by default crates.io) — a publication that reaches the registry and its downstream users. This is the *default* behavior; `cargo publish --dry-run` performs the same packaging and verification but does NOT upload, reporting what would be published instead. This note names the possible publication effect; it is documentation, not an authorization — the lookup neither authorizes nor performs a publication.

commands.purpose: Display the active toolchain, the installed toolchains, and the active override for the current directory.
examples: `rustup show` prints the active toolchain (channel, host, release), the installed toolchains, and any directory override in force; `rustup show --active-toolchain` prints only the active toolchain name.
prerequisites: `rustup` is installed (the Rust toolchain installer); the active toolchain is the one the installer selected or pinned for the directory.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `rustup`; run `rustup show --help` for the version-specific option list. The help/version mechanism is `rustup --help`, `rustup --version`, and `rustup show --active-toolchain` (which reports the toolchain name for the current directory).

When the active toolchain's version is unknown or differs from the documented baseline, report the version `rustup show` actually returns rather than assuming a documented version applies; that version-qualification is preserved, not flattened to an unconditional claim. Retrieving this entry is documentation lookup: it surfaces toolchain-inspection guidance and does not change the toolchain; the calling agent decides whether to run `rustup show` through its own terminal tools.

commands.purpose: Install, link, list, or set the active Rust toolchain.
examples: `rustup toolchain install stable` installs the stable toolchain; `rustup toolchain install nightly` installs a nightly channel; `rustup toolchain link my-toolchain /path/to/rustc` registers a local toolchain; `rustup toolchain use stable` makes a channel the active toolchain for the current directory.
prerequisites: `rustup` is installed; installing or linking a toolchain may fetch it from a configured toolchain source.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `rustup`; run `rustup toolchain --help` for the version-specific option list. The help/version mechanism is `rustup toolchain --help` (and `rustup --version` for the installer version); channel availability (for example `nightly`) is documented per channel, and the stable/nightly qualification is preserved, not flattened to unconditional.

Retrieving this entry is documentation lookup: it surfaces toolchain-management guidance and does not install, link, or switch a toolchain. No toolchain is changed as a result of this lookup; the calling agent decides whether to run `rustup toolchain` through its own terminal tools.

effect_notes.detail: changes the user's rustup toolchain state: `install`/`link` add a toolchain (a possible download of the toolchain sources), and `use`/`override` change the active toolchain for a directory. This note names the possible toolchain change; it is documentation, not a permission to make the change.

commands.purpose: Set, list, or remove the directory toolchain override.
examples: `rustup override set nightly` pins the current directory to the nightly toolchain; `rustup override list` shows the directory overrides; `rustup override unset` removes them. A `rust-toolchain.toml` file in the directory pins the toolchain, overrides, and components in place.
prerequisites: `rustup` is installed; `rustup override set` requires the referenced toolchain to be installed (or it is fetched).
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `rustup`; run `rustup override --help` for the version-specific option list. The help/version mechanism is `rustup override --help`; the override channel (for example `nightly`) is documented per channel and its stable/nightly qualification is preserved, not flattened.

Retrieving this entry is documentation lookup: it surfaces override-management guidance and does not set, list, or remove an override. No directory override is changed as a result of this lookup; the calling agent decides whether to run `rustup override` through its own terminal tools.

effect_notes.detail: `rustup override set` writes a directory override into rustup's override store (or a `rust-toolchain.toml` file), changing which toolchain runs in that directory; `unset` removes it. This note names the possible toolchain change; it is documentation, not a permission to make the change.

commands.purpose: Add, remove, or list the components of a toolchain.
examples: `rustup component add rustfmt clippy` installs the rustfmt and Clippy components for the active toolchain; `rustup component list` shows the installed, available, and up-to-date components; `rustup component remove rustfmt` uninstalls a component.
prerequisites: `rustup` is installed with an active toolchain; adding a component may fetch it from the configured component source.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `rustup`; run `rustup component --help` for the version-specific option list. The help/version mechanism is `rustup component --help`; component availability varies by channel and host, and that qualification is preserved, not flattened to unconditional.

Retrieving this entry is documentation lookup: it surfaces component-management guidance and does not add or remove a component. No component is installed or removed as a result of this lookup; the calling agent decides whether to run `rustup component` through its own terminal tools.

effect_notes.detail: `rustup component add`/`remove` change which components are installed for the active toolchain (a possible download when adding). This note names the possible toolchain change; it is documentation, not a permission to make the change.

commands.purpose: Add, list, or remove target triples for a toolchain.
examples: `rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` makes a target triple available for cross-compilation; `rustup target list --installed` shows the installed targets; `rustup target remove x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` removes one.
prerequisites: `rustup` is installed with an active toolchain; adding a target may fetch it from the configured target source.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `rustup`; run `rustup target --help` for the version-specific option list. The help/version mechanism is `rustup target --help`; which target triples are available varies by host and channel, and that qualification is preserved, not flattened to unconditional.

Retrieving this entry is documentation lookup: it surfaces target-management guidance and does not add or remove a target. No target triple is changed as a result of this lookup; the calling agent decides whether to run `rustup target` through its own terminal tools.

effect_notes.detail: `rustup target add`/`remove` change which target triples are available for the active toolchain (a possible download when adding). This note names the possible toolchain change; it is documentation, not a permission to make the change.

commands.purpose: The Rust compiler; document its usage, options, and flags.
examples: `rustc main.rs --edition 2021` compiles `main.rs` using edition 2021; `rustc --version` prints the compiler version; `rustc --help` (and `rustc -Z help` on a nightly build) lists the options.
prerequisites: A Rust compiler (`rustc`) is installed, typically as part of a toolchain managed by `rustup`; the edition and options used must be supported by the installed compiler.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `rustc`; run `rustc --help` for the version-specific option list. The help/version mechanism is `rustc --help` and `rustc --version`; `--edition` selects the language edition the compiler supports.

Some `rustc` options are unstable or nightly-only; the documentation marks them as such and `rustc -Z help` (on a nightly build) lists the unstable options. A documented unstable/nightly-only option keeps its `nightly`/`unstable` qualification — it is not flattened to an unconditional claim that it is available on every build. When the installed compiler's version is unknown or differs from the documented baseline, consult the version that is installed rather than assuming the documented options apply; that version-qualification is preserved.

effect_notes.detail: `rustc` compiles its input and writes the compilation output (a binary, object file, or library — a build artifact) under the working directory or `target/`. It compiles a single crate; it does not execute the project's own code as its defining effect. This note names the possible artifact write; it is documentation, not a permission to run `rustc`.

commands.purpose: The Rust code formatter; document its usage and configuration.
examples: `rustfmt src/main.rs` formats the file in place; `rustfmt --check src/main.rs` reports formatting differences without writing; a `rustfmt.toml` file (or `--config`) sets per-project options.
prerequisites: The `rustfmt` binary is installed, typically as the `rustfmt` component of a toolchain (for example via `rustup component add rustfmt`).
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `rustfmt`; run `rustfmt --help` for the version-specific option list. The help/version mechanism is `rustfmt --help` and `rustfmt --version`; `--check` runs in check mode and `--config` selects an option.

Unstable rustfmt options require a nightly `rustfmt` (selected via `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=nightly` or `RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=1`); a documented unstable option keeps its `unstable`/`nightly` qualification — it is not flattened to an unconditional claim that it works on a stable `rustfmt`. When the installed `rustfmt`'s version is unknown or differs from the documented baseline, consult the version that is installed; that version-qualification is preserved.

effect_notes.detail: `rustfmt` reformats the target source files in place (a source change); `rustfmt --check` only checks formatting and does not write. This note names the possible source change; it is documentation, not a permission to run `rustfmt`.

commands.purpose: The Rust documentation generator; document its usage and configuration.
examples: `rustdoc src/lib.rs` generates HTML documentation; `rustdoc --document-private-items` also documents private items; `rustdoc --check` runs the documentation tests (doctests) only, and `cargo test --doc` does the same for a package.
prerequisites: The `rustdoc` binary is installed, typically as part of a toolchain (the `rust-docs` component enables rendering of intra-doc links); a library or binary crate is documented as input.
compatibility: Syntax and options are documented for the installed `rustdoc`; run `rustdoc --help` for the version-specific option list. The help/version mechanism is `rustdoc --help` and `rustdoc --version`; `--document-private-items` is documented and stable, while some other rustdoc options are unstable.

Some rustdoc options are unstable and require a nightly toolchain (for example via `RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=1` or `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=nightly`); a documented unstable/nightly-only option keeps its `nightly`/`unstable` qualification — it is not flattened to an unconditional claim that it is available on a stable build. When the installed `rustdoc`'s version is unknown or differs from the documented baseline, consult the version that is installed; that version-qualification is preserved.

effect_notes.detail: `rustdoc` writes an HTML documentation tree under `target/doc` (a documentation artifact); with `--check` it runs the documentation tests and reports without writing the tree. This note names the possible artifact write; it is documentation, not a permission to run `rustdoc`.
